DOI 10.5788/31-1-1643 (open-access publisher PDF, lexikos.journals.ac.za). Corroboration: Uguru & Okeke 2020, Lexikos 30: 537; Kareem & Maikanti 2024, JSMULA 12(2): 586 (second-hand from Obisesan 2012); Eleshin-Ajikobi 2025, JLLLS 5(1): 20.
catalog_locator: sec. 3.2 'Prosody', 3.2.1 'Tone' and 3.2.2 'Stress and syllabic structure', pp. 222-223 of (re- with)
catalog_quote: 3.2.1 Tone Adeshokan (2018) reveals that just like in Spanish, accents feature in Lukumi words. Tone, a feature of Yoruba, the parent language, does not feature in Lukumi but it exists in Olukumi. 3.2.2 Stress and syllabic structure Lukumi words are not tone marked but rather accents (typical of Spanish) are used to indicate stressed syllables and they usually occur in word final position (Ramos 2012; Concordia 2012). As can be observed from the data, Lukumi and Olukumi have CV syllable structure. Hence they do not have closed syllables. Spanish has a closed syllable structure but that did not influence Lukumi.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Olukumi is described as a tone language (it keeps the Yoruba tone system; a second open source, Kareem & Maikanti 2024 p. 586 reporting Obisesan 2012, gives the tones as high, low, mid; Eleshin-Ajikobi 2025 shows mid vs high-low on final syllables). No source opened says anything about word stress in Olukumi: Uguru's 'Stress' subsection attributes word-final accent/stress to Lukumi (the Cuban ritual variety) only, contrasting it with tonal Olukumi.
new_statements.exceptions: None; the source contrasts Olukumi (tone) with Lukumi (Spanish-type word-final stress accents).
new_statements.domain_note: Lexical items elicited for a multilingual dictionary (word level, citation forms); Uguru places the Olukumi data in Delta State (she says Oshimili LGA; other sources: Aniocha North LGA, Ugbodu and Ukwu-Nzu varieties).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Olùkùmi/Ulukwumi of Delta State (uluk1257); Eleshin-Ajikobi 2025 and the Talking/Living Dictionaries use the Ugbodu variety (Arokoyo 2020 distinguishes Ugbodu, closer to Yoruba, from Ukwu-Nzu, heavily Igbo-influenced). Uguru 2021 locates her Olukumi data in 'Oshimili Local Government Area', but the language is otherwise placed in Aniocha North LGA. Do not confuse with Lukumi/Anagó of Cuba (lucu1238), the other variety in Uguru's comparison, which is the one her stress statement is about.
